prime.problem: First Missing Positive asks for O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Sorting is O(n log n), and a set is O(n) memory. Something has to play the role of a hash table without allocating one.
prime.fits: Closes the Sorting part. After the n log n card showed sorting's floor, this card beats it by using the value range: like radix sort, it computes each value's position from the value itself, but in one pass and in place.
expect: swap until home or out of range
each swap settles one value for good
prime.goal: Trace cyclic placement, prove its nested loop is O(n), and recognise the "values are a permutation of 1 … n" family of problems.

attend: Why can the answer only be in 1 … n + 1, and why does that make values ≤ 0 or > n irrelevant?
Why does a value, once in its home slot, never move again?
The loop is a while inside a for. What bounds the total number of swaps at n?
Why must the guard be nums[v − 1] != v and not v != i + 1?
Why does the Python one-line swap loop forever here?

must: n numbers can cover at most 1 … n → the answer is in 1 … n + 1 → only values in 1 … n matter → each has a unique home v − 1, so the array itself is a collision-free hash table
A swap happens only when slot v − 1 doesn't hold v, and afterwards it does → no swap ever evicts a value from its home → ≤ n swaps in total, ≤ 2n while-checks → O(n) despite the nested loop
After placement, the first slot i without i + 1 names the missing value → O(1) extra space → but the input is reordered, so it only fits when mutation is allowed
elevated: Guard on the destination (nums[v − 1] != v) → a duplicate stops when its home is already taken → guarding on the source (v != i + 1) makes two equal values swap forever
Python evaluates nums[i], nums[nums[i] - 1] = … left to right, so the second target uses the new nums[i] → read j = nums[i] − 1 first
reference: the 99,988 swaps / 12 cycles figure for a shuffled 10⁵

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory: why the answer lies in 1 … n + 1, what the placement loop does, why it's O(n) despite nesting, and how you read the answer off.
checklist: pigeonhole: n values can fill at most 1 … n
send each v in range to slot v − 1 by swapping; ignore the rest
each swap settles one value permanently, so ≤ n swaps
first slot i with nums[i] ≠ i + 1 → answer i + 1, else n + 1
O(1) extra space, but mutates the input; guard against duplicates

retrieve.q: Explain why the cyclic placement loop is O(n) even though the inner while can run several times for one i.
answer: every swap puts some value into its home slot, where it stays forever
there are at most n values in 1 … n, so at most n swaps overall
each check either swaps or advances i, so ≤ 2n checks

retrieve.q: Trace [3, 4, −1, 1] at i = 1: which checks happen, which swaps, and why does i = 1 swap twice before moving on?
answer: check 5: v = −1 is out of range → advance
the 1 that arrived from slot 3 wasn't home yet, so the while keeps going

retrieve.q: The input array is read-only (it's shared with another thread). What do you use instead, and what does the choice cost?
answer: copying it to use cyclic placement costs O(n) space anyway
so use a set of the values and test 1, 2, 3 …: O(n) time, O(n) space
or, if exactly one value is missing from 0 … n, the sum formula needs no extra space and no mutation

compare.q: A Python set and this trick both answer "is v present?" in O(1). What does each use as the hash function and table, which design choice removes collisions here, and what does each cost?
answer: the set hashes arbitrary values into its own table, handling collisions; O(n) extra memory
here hash(v) = v − 1 and the input is the table; distinct values in 1 … n never collide
the trick needs a bounded value range and a mutable input; the set needs neither

compare.q: Both move values by swapping. Why is insertion sort's swap count up to n(n − 1)/2 while cyclic placement's is at most n?
answer: insertion sort moves a value one slot per swap, so a value far from home pays its whole distance
cyclic placement sends a value straight to its computed home in one swap
knowing the destination from the value itself is what removes the distance cost

predict.q: What does the algorithm return for [1, 1, 2, 2], and how many swaps does it make? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: Answer 3, after 1 swap. At i = 0, 1 is home. At i = 1, v = 1 but slot 0 already holds 1: the guard stops (no swap). At i = 2, v = 2 and slot 1 holds 1 → swap → [1, 2, 1, 2]; now slot 2 holds 1, whose home is taken → stop. At i = 3, 2's home holds 2 → stop. Scan: slot 2 holds 1 ≠ 3 → return 3.

apply.task: Trace [7, 1, 2, 5, 3] check by check. Write the array after each swap and the swap count, then read off the answer. Then trace [3, 1, 2] and explain why it returns n + 1.
apply.done: The first array ends as [1, 2, 3, 7, 5] after 4 swaps and returns 4 (slot 3 holds the out-of-range 7). The second ends as [1, 2, 3] after 2 swaps (both at i = 0) and returns 4 = n + 1, because every slot holds its own number.
apply.hint: 7 is out of range for n = 5 and never moves on purpose; it ends in the one slot no in-range value claims.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the answer for [1, 1, 2, 2], or the number of swaps?
Could you explain the ≤ n swaps bound without the word "amortized"?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: pigeonhole → value range, or home slot → no evictions?
Which related problems (all duplicates, all missing numbers, set mismatch) could you now solve with the same loop?
What will you look for in the Searching part: other ways a known structure lets you skip work?
